title: Are you getting these wrong too? | EGGCORNS

entries.note: A mistaken but sensible-sounding word substitute; named by [[see:Geoffrey Pullum]] after a letter calling [[from:acorn]]s egg corns, shared by [[see:Chris Potts]] with [[see:Mark Liberman]].
An eggcorn for [[from:damp squib]].
An eggcorn for [[from:nip it in the bud]]; Jess admits she long thought it was the logical version.
The correct form of [[gave:nip it in the butt]], referring to clipping a bud off a plant.
An eggcorn for [[from:expatriate]] that Jess hears around her.
Spelling confused with [[see:praying mantis]], seen in writing, mixing up preying as hunting with praying in the religious sense.
Contrasted with [[see:preying mantis]]: praying in the religious sense rather than preying as in hunting.
An eggcorn Rob made all his life, as if about a king's reign, for [[from:free rein]].
Refers to allowing a horse enough rein, not royal power; often miswritten as [[gave:free reign]].
So widespread an eggcorn for [[from:champing at the bit]] that few notice it, since a horse champing at the bit is also chomping.
The original of [[gave:chomping at the bit]]; the bit is the piece in a horse's mouth.
No longer used as a verb, so most people think it means champion, prompting [[see:chomping at the bit]].
A child's eggcorn for [[from:Alzheimer's disease]], logical because it mostly affects elderly people.
A medical eggcorn for [[from:migraines]].
A medical eggcorn for [[from:post-traumatic stress disorder]].
A medical eggcorn for [[from:carpal tunnel syndrome]] that Rob read online.
A common medical eggcorn for [[from:chickenpox]], usually from children.
A viewer's aunt said a relative was in tense of care, an eggcorn for [[from:intensive care]].
An eggcorn for [[from:for all intents and purposes]], which people sometimes use deliberately.
Misheard as egg corn in a letter about acorns falling on a car, giving [[gave:eggcorn]]; in some accents the two sound identical.
Jess had only read it and thought it was pronounced differently; it means looking sideways at someone suspiciously.
A word Rob mispronounced in his head from reading it, a common case because the a- construction looks odd.
The prefix in [[see:askance]] and [[see:awry]], rarely used now; Jess thinks it shows Old Norse influence and may relate to [[same-root?:ado]].
A contraction of at do, reflecting a Norse infinitive marker cognate with English at, rather than to do.
A common eggcorn for [[from:bald-faced lie]], falsely explained as referring to bold headline type.
The original form, like [[equivalent:barefaced lie]]: lying to someone's face with your face uncovered, without it showing.
A correct alternative to [[equivalent:bald-faced lie]].
An American term for a celebrity that baffled Rob in a newsroom script; Jess suggests a name worthy of bolding.
An eggcorn for [[from:wreak havoc]], arising because wreak is rarely used now.
Wreak means to cause or inflict, from an Old English word meaning to avenge or drive out, surviving mainly here and in wreaking revenge.
An eggcorn for [[from:whet your appetite]], making sense through the image of a watering mouth.
Uses a sword-sharpening metaphor, as with a [[see:whetstone]].
A stone used to sharpen a sword, explaining [[see:whet your appetite]]; Jess meets it in fantasy fiction.
Named as another eggcorn, for [[from:brass tacks]].
Named as another eggcorn, for [[from:pass muster]].
Used in be weary of instead of [[see:wary]]; Rob wonders if it is an eggcorn, a malapropism or just a wrong word.
An older word meaning to be cautious, often replaced by [[see:weary]].
A misspelling of [[from:bated breath]] as in fishing bait, perhaps imagining something catching in the throat.
From [[from:abate]], to reduce or end, so breath is halting; bated is a [[see:fossil words]] example.
Words that survive in no other context, so speakers cannot work them out, causing many eggcorns like [[see:bated breath]].
A Latin-derived word now used in contexts where abate, the source of [[see:bated breath]], once was.
Rob says he gets corrected on how he pronounces it.
An eggcorn for [[from:moot point]], complained about on a 1978 BBC Radio 4 show, proving such errors aren't new.
The correct form behind [[gave:mute point]].
Like eggcorns but goofier, making far less sense; named after [[from:Mrs Malaprop]].
Character in [[see:Richard Brinsley Sheridan]]'s 1775 play The Rivals, named from French [[from:mal à propos]], who misuses grandiloquent words; Fowler called her matron saint of word-fowlers.
[[see:Mrs Malaprop]]'s malapropism for the pinnacle of politeness.
[[see:Mrs Malaprop]]'s malapropism for it gives me the hysterics.
From Jess's favourite [[see:Mrs Malaprop]] quote, meaning a nice arrangement of epithets, ironically claiming mastery of language.

entries.term: headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile
entries.note: [[see:Mrs Malaprop]]'s malapropism, using allegory for alligator.
A misheard lyric, named after Lady Mondegreen, a mishearing of laid him on the green in [[from:The Bonnie Earl o' Moray]].
Scottish folk song whose line laid him on the green was misheard, giving [[gave:mondegreen]].
Rob's mondegreen of Ciao adios, I'm done from Anne-Marie's song Ciao Adios.

entries.term: taking the horse to the hotel room
entries.note: Rob's mondegreen of a lyric in Lil Nas X's Old Town Road.
Jess's childhood mishearing of Latin church songs, wondering who at Chelsea was, from in excelsis Deo.

entries.term: excuse me while I kiss this guy
entries.note: Famous mondegreen of [[see:Jimi Hendrix]]'s excuse me while I kiss the sky.
Means to momentarily forget something, as in a test; same term as the historical [[see:Iron Curtain]], commonly eggcorned as [[gave:få hjerneteppe]].
The historical Iron Curtain shares its term with Norwegian [[see:få jernteppe]].
A classic Norwegian eggcorn for [[from:få jernteppe]].
Spanish for making a scene, from [[from:poyo]]; once meaning to embarrass someone, now often written [[gave:montar un pollo]].
A rarely used word for a podium that judges and orators climbed to speak, found in [[see:montar un poyo]].
The modern Spanish eggcorn written for [[from:montar un poyo]].
Means to uncover a secret; the rose pot held ladies' perfumes; often misheard as [[gave:découvrir le pot rose]].
A French mishearing of [[from:découvrir le pot aux roses]] that Rob jokes sounds like a filthy euphemism.
A Twitter mangling of [[from:bon appétit]] that names a subreddit of malapropisms; Rob thinks it reflects American pronunciation.
Used on Bone Apple Tea in place of [[see:capybara]] under a capybara picture.
Used on Bone Apple Tea in place of [[see:laminate]], the plastic over paper.
Jess's favourite Bone Apple Tea malapropism, for [[from:rotisserie]] chicken.
Nobody, including Mark Liberman, knows whether this or [[see:buck naked]] is correct; both work.
Rival of [[see:butt naked]]; Jess believes it is a racist Americanism about Native Americans, perhaps referencing buckskin.
Rob's long-running error for [[from:painstaking]], as if staking pain.
Comes from taking pains, which Rob had never connected.
Rob's eggcorn for [[from:down the pike]].
The correct form of [[gave:down the pipe]].
Rob thought of edible desserts, not things you deserve, a homophone of [[see:just deserts]].
Means things you deserve, misunderstood as [[see:just desserts]].
